semantic_correction.stem: A dying client tells the nurse that a specific family ritual should occur immediately after death and asks that several relatives be present. The request differs from the unit's usual practice. What is the nurse's best response?

options.A: Explain that the unit's standard post-death routine generally takes priority, then discuss alternatives with the family later if the requested ritual cannot be incorporated.
options.B: Ask the client to explain the ritual and who should participate, document the preferences, and communicate them to the care team so they can be accommodated when feasible.
options.C: Arrange the customary ritual associated with the client's cultural or religious group without asking more questions, because group traditions usually define the needed care.
options.D: Defer discussion of post-death rituals until after death, because end-of-life planning should focus on care provided while the client is still alive.

semantic_correction.rationale: B is correct. Current National Institute on Aging guidance states that the health care team should understand how a person's cultural and religious background may influence end-of-life expectations, needs, and choices and encourages families to discuss personal and family traditions with the health care team. NIA also states that an end-of-life care plan may include wishes for what happens after death. The nurse should therefore clarify the client's own preferences rather than assume what the ritual involves, document those wishes, and communicate them to the interdisciplinary team so the plan can honor them as much as possible within safety, legal, and organizational constraints. A is incorrect because routine unit practice should not automatically override individualized cultural or religious wishes. C is incorrect because it stereotypes the client by assuming that every member of a cultural or religious group follows the same ritual. D is incorrect because NIA explicitly includes after-death wishes in end-of-life care planning, so the discussion should occur before death when the client can express preferences.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Individualize end-of-life care by eliciting, documenting, and communicating the client's stated cultural or religious preferences, including wishes for what should occur after death, rather than imposing routine practice or making assumptions based on group identity.
semantic_correction.source_organization: National Institute on Aging (NIA), National Institutes of Health
semantic_correction.source_document_title: Making Decisions for Someone at the End of Life
semantic_correction.source_version_date: Content reviewed November 17, 2022; NIA states that scientists and other experts review the content for accuracy and currency; current page accessed August 21, 2026
semantic_correction.source_locator: Cultural considerations at the end of life: everyone involved in care should understand how a person's history and cultural and religious background may influence end-of-life expectations, needs, and choices; discuss personal and family traditions surrounding end of life with the health care team; communicate what is important ahead of time. Discussing a care plan: an end-of-life care plan helps ensure the person's wishes are respected as much as possible and may include wishes after death, such as funeral arrangements and what will be done with the body.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: NIA supports discussing individualized cultural and religious end-of-life traditions with the health care team and including after-death wishes in the care plan so the person's preferences can be respected as much as possible.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: removed the conspicuous absolute-word distractor and correct-answer length cue, added explicit feasibility limits to avoid promising unrestricted accommodation, and rebuilt all four responses as balanced end-of-life planning actions.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests individualized, culturally responsive end-of-life planning without stereotyping or overpromising, with one clearly best nursing response and no conspicuous cueing.

option_audit.A: Incorrect. It gives routine unit practice presumptive priority rather than first eliciting and communicating the client's stated wishes for individualized planning.
option_audit.B: Correct. It directly reflects NIA guidance to clarify personal traditions, communicate what matters, and include after-death wishes in the care plan while allowing for feasibility constraints.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. It substitutes a group-based assumption for assessment of the individual client's preferences and risks stereotyping.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. NIA states that end-of-life care planning may include wishes for what happens after death, so postponing the discussion until after death defeats advance planning.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. B alone combines individualized assessment, documentation, communication, and feasible accommodation; A prematurely subordinates the client's preferences to routine, C stereotypes, and D improperly delays planning until the client can no longer participate.
cueing_check: All four choices are parallel nursing responses of comparable length and specificity; the prior 'must' wording and uniquely-long correct answer were removed, and no option is structurally privileged by formatting.
